Plus: Gold is back | Thursday, August 13, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Aug 13, 2026
 
 
 🏋🏻‍♂️ Hey everybody, we're really powering through this week. 

 📈 U.S. stock futures are positive this morning after yesterday's relatively benign inflation print — and there's more pricing data on the way with the Producer Price Index for July out at 8:30am. 

 🤑 Anthropic's investors told the Financial Times that they expect the AI darling to float at an eye-watering $2 trillion+ valuation in October. Today, Matt zooms in on those CoreWeave earnings that catapulted the stock up nearly 20% yesterday. Turns out, its losses are getting larger, and the company is having trouble making it up on volume. Plus, Emily dives into the gold market like a youthful Scrooge McDuck. Keep it locked! In 752 words, a 3-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: 🧺 The CoreWeave conundrum
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Note: Loss data is produced in accordance with GAAP; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios CoreWeave's losses doubled, its spending soared, and it devoured almost $6 billion more in cash than it generated last quarter. Investors loved it. 

 Why it matters: Some see CoreWeave, a so-called neocloud that builds data centers and sells AI computing power, as the canary in the coal mine of the AI trade. 

 After the report, that canary was tweeting and flying high. The latest: Shares of the neocloud soared 19% after it reported second-quarter results the previous evening.

 CoreWeave's numbers were broadly consistent with what we've been hearing from hyperscalers and others. Sales and backlog showed rising demand for AI compute, as revenue more than doubled, to $2.58 billion. Remaining performance obligations, a measure of sales backlog, jumped 245% to $103.7 billion. Yes, but: The company's losses are getting deeper for every dollar of sales it collects. 

 Its adjusted net loss worsened to $567 million from $130 million during the same quarter last year. (According to stricter GAAP accounting rules, the loss was worse, $626 million.) CoreWeave's adjusted net loss margin — or how much it loses for every dollar of sales, excluding certain items — declined to -22% from -11%. And the company's free cash flow, considered one of the highest-quality earnings indicators, was negative $5.74 billion, a sharp deterioration from negative $2.70 billion the previous year, according to FactSet. Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios What they're saying: Bulls are keeping the faith, while skeptics are, um, skeptical. 

 "Overall, results/guide reflect a robust demand/constrained supply backdrop that should continue to drive revenue growth/margin expansion momentum," Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani wrote. "While guidance went up on every line," wrote Madison Rezaei, an analyst with Bernstein Research. "Capex went up higher than all of them." "We're still not fans of the model," she later added. Between the lines: While some deference to the market's reaction may be due, that should likely come with a few grains of salt as well. 

 The most recent data showed more than 20% of CoreWeave's float in the hands of short sellers. Since shorts have to buy the stock to exit, or cover, their trades, a move higher in a heavily shorted stock like CoreWeave can create a mad rush to exit positions, generating something known as a squeeze. That could be part of what's happened with the stock yesterday. The bottom line: If one wants a clean read on CoreWeave, it could be illustrative to take a look at what insiders have been doing recently with their holdings. 

 As the chart below shows, what they definitely haven't been doing is buying — at least in the aggregate — and that's pretty interesting in itself. Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

2. 💛 Gold is regaining luster
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios Gold prices rose to their highest level in more than two months yesterday — hitting $4,465 an ounce.

 Why it matters: The precious metal has reversed a slump that began shortly after the start of the war with Iran.

 It's a sign that inflation expectations are easing. Flashback: Investors expected inflation and real yields to rise when the war started, which made gold — a non-yielding asset — less appealing, and undermined the notion that it behaves as a safe asset in turbulent times.

 State of play: But after the most recent meeting of Federal Reserve policymakers, at the end of July, investors got a " dovish surprise " — and gold began its ascent. 

 Yesterday's relatively benign CPI report offered more assurance. Follow the money: There might be an even simpler explanation for gold's leg up: China reported buying nearly 20 metric tons of gold in July, its largest purchase since October 2023. 

 Nothing like more demand to add a little polish to prices.
